query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Processing single‐phase ZrB2 by ultra‐high pressure sintering (UHPS) at substantially lower temperatures (around 1450 °C) will induce severe plastic deformation that refines the grain size and multiplies dislocations; these microstructural changes will simultaneously improve mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and liquid-metal corrosion durability compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 powder typically requiring sintering above 1700–2300 °C
generation.intervention: Implement UHPS by sintering the ZrB2 powder under pressures around 15 GPa at a much lower temperature (~1450 °C) for a short duration (e.g., 10 minutes)
generation.conditions: Sintering carried out at approximately 1450 °C under ultra-high pressure (≈15 GPa) for a controlled short holding time; subsequent service in high-temperature oxidation and liquid metal environments
generation.structural_mediator: Severe plastic deformation induces grain refinement and a high density of dislocations and substructures
generation.mechanism: Under ultra-high pressure, plastic deformation promotes dislocation multiplication and grain-boundary sliding, resulting in nano-scaled grains. The refined grain structure and high dislocation density improve mechanical strength (via Hall–Petch and Taylor hardening effects) and enable the formation of a more stable, protective oxide scale that delays oxidation and resists corrosion from liquid plating metals.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventional ZrB2 specimens sintered at higher temperatures (≥1700 °C), the UHPS-processed ZrB2 should exhibit a roughly 40–50% increase in hardness, a near 70% improvement in fracture toughness, and an increase in the threshold oxidation temperature by approximately 250 °C. These improvements should also translate to enhanced durability in liquid metal plating environments.
generation.baseline: Conventional sintering methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering or hot-pressing) at temperatures above 1700 °C yield coarser grain structures with lower dislocation densities and inferior oxidation/corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The performance benefits are expected under the specific UHPS conditions (≈15 GPa, ~1450 °C, short hold time). Scalability or differing pressure/temperature regimes may not reproduce the same microstructural benefits, and actual service performance in specific liquid metal baths must be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While laboratory-scale UHPS has shown promising results, the practical scalability, uniformity in larger components, and exact quantitative performance improvements under industrial liquid plating conditions require further experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 specimens: one set processed via UHPS (15 GPa at 1450 °C for 10 minutes) and a control set processed conventionally (e.g., SPS at 2000 °C). Expose both sets to cyclic oxidation tests and a controlled liquid metal plating bath environment. Evaluate and compare mechanical properties and oxidation/corrosion resistance.
measurements: Grain size and dislocation density (via SEM/TEM)
Threshold oxidation temperature (using thermogravimetric analysis or similar)
Mass loss or corrosion rate during liquid metal plating tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UHPS-processed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 40% increase in hardness, roughly a 70% increase in toughness, and a ~250 °C higher oxidation threshold, along with lower mass loss during liquid metal plating) compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In summary, fully‐dense and finer‐grained ultra‐high temperature ZrB2 ceramics were successfully fabricated under ultra‐high pressure at low temperature. The dominant densification mechanism was proposed and proved as the plastic deformation‐induced dislocation multiplication and grain boundary sliding. The proportion of dislocation cells, substructures, and small‐angle grain boundaries gradually increased when the sintering temperature reached the critical temperature of 1450 °C. ZrB2 sintered under 15 GPa at the optimized temperature of 1450 °C holding 10 min showed full density, fine microstructures, high dislocation density, and excellent mechanical properties. The grain size of as‐sintered ZrB2 ceramics decreased ≈56% compared with the raw powder. The microstructure observation after indentation and properties characterization after heat treatment proved that the high dislocation density, finer grain size, and high prestress induced by UHPS contributed the enhancement of mechanical properties.
